lifeOsSource.hack: Set a short timer and clear only the items that are blocking your immediate work. Put obvious items back, remove trash, and stop when the timer ends.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Set a short timer and tidy one small part of your workspace. Make only obvious moves, then stop before tidying turns into a larger task.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Is the workspace easier to use now, and did I stop before tidying became a new form of procrastination?

faq.question: Does it need to be exactly two minutes?
faq.answer: No. Two minutes is simply a small boundary. Use a short period that helps you reset the workspace without turning the reset into a cleaning project.

faq.question: What should I tidy first?
faq.answer: Start with obvious items: trash, cups, tools with a clear home, or objects physically blocking the work you want to do next. Leave complicated filing decisions for another time.

faq.question: What if the workspace needs a full cleanup?
faq.answer: Use the short reset only to make the next task easier. If deeper cleaning is needed, schedule it separately so the quick reset does not consume the work block.

intro.html: A short desk reset can be useful when clutter is physically getting in the way or when you want a clear transition into the next task. The point is not to create a perfect workspace. It is to remove a little friction and then get back to the work that matters.

sections.title: 1. Choose one small area
sections.html: Pick the part of the workspace you need for the next task: the keyboard area, one corner of the desk, or the space around your notebook. Do not expand the scope to the whole room.

sections.title: 2. Set a short boundary
sections.html: Use a short timer if it helps you stop. Two minutes is a convenient default, not a proven optimum. A shorter or slightly longer reset is fine if it keeps the task small.

sections.title: 3. Make only obvious moves
sections.html: Throw away trash, move a cup, return an item that has a clear home, or stack papers that are blocking the surface. Avoid opening drawers, redesigning storage, or starting decisions that need more thought.

sections.title: 4. Stop when the reset is enough
sections.html: When the timer ends, stop unless there is one immediate safety or cleanup issue. A tidy desk can become another avoidance task surprisingly quickly, because apparently humans can procrastinate by becoming extremely interested in cable management.

sections.title: 5. Start the real task
sections.html: Open the document, tool, or material you actually planned to use. The reset has done its job when the next useful action is easier to begin.

sections.title: 6. Review whether it helped
sections.html: After a few uses, ask whether the reset is helping you start work or simply adding another ritual. Keep it only if it earns its place.
